'''''Petrosedum forsterianum''''', the '''rock stonecrop''' or '''Welsh stonecrop''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Crassulaceae]]. It is a mat-forming, evergreen [[stonecrop]] native to northwestern and southwestern Europe and northern Africa. It may be grown as an [[ornamental plant]] or consumed.
==Distribution==
The natural range of ''Petrosedum forsterianum'' includes England, Wales, Ireland, France, Germany, Spain, and Portugal (including the [[Azores]]), as well as Morocco. It thrives in rocky habitats, forming dense, low-growing mats.<ref name="Eggli">{{cite book | last=Eggli | first=Urs | title=Illustrated Handbook of Succulent Plants: Crassulaceae | publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg | year=2012 | isbn=978-3-642-55874-0 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nU7mCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA201 | access-date=2 February 2025 | page=267}}</ref> It is often found in the shaded [[edge habitat|edges]] of glades.<ref name="Stephenson"/> It is common in the shade of shrubs, which initially serve as [[nurse plant]]s and then provide partial shade for mature specimens.<ref name="Smith"/>

==Taxonomy==
''Petrosedum forsterianum'' was originally described as ''Sedum forsterianum'' and formerly considered a [[subspecies]] of ''[[Sedum rupestre]]'' (nowadays ''Petrosedum rupestre''). ''P. rupestre'' and ''P. forsterianum'' are still frequently confused.<ref name="Stephenson"/> The [[specific epithet]] honors [[Edward Forster the Younger]].<ref name="Newton">{{cite book | last1=Eggli | first1=Urs | last2=Newton | first2=Leonard E. | title=Etymological Dictionary of Succulent Plant Names | publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg | year=2013 | isbn=978-3-662-07125-0 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gf3uCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA86 | access-date=10 February 2025 | page=86}}</ref>

Over time, different names have been used to describe various forms of ''Petrosedum forsterianum'', but [[Henk 't Hart]] (1978) observed that these forms exist along a continuous gradient rather than as clearly defined categories. [[Louis-Paul Hébert]] recorded that all [[octoploid]] types occur north of the [[Pyrenees]].<ref name="Stephenson"/> A naturally occurring [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] between ''[[Petrosedum sediforme]]'' and ''P. forsterianum'' was discovered in Portugal and described in 2015 as ''[[Petrosedum × estrelae]]''.<ref name="Smith">{{cite journal | last1=Smith | first1=Gideon F. |last2=Stephenson | first2=Ray | title=''Petrosedum×estrelae'' Gideon F.Sm. & R.Stephenson (Crassulaceae) [''Petrosedum forsterianum'' (Sm.) Grulich × ''Petrosedum sediforme'' (Jacq.) Grulich]: a new nothospecies from central Portugal | journal=Bradleya | publisher=British Cactus and Succulent Society | volume=33 | issue=33 | date=20 October 2015 | issn=0265-086X | doi=10.25223/brad.n33.2015.a2 | pages=2–8| bibcode=2015Bradl..33....2S }}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Sedum forsterianum 2017-04-17 7599.jpg|thumb|left|''P. forsterianum'' has creeping shoots, like these, and upright flowering shoots.]]
''Petrosedum forsterianum'' has two types of [[shoot (botany)|shoots]]: creeping, non-flowering ones that take root as they spread, and upright, flowering stems. The non-flowering shoots have tightly packed, scale-like leaves clustered at their tips, giving them a cone-like appearance. These leaves are linear in shape, slightly rounded or somewhat flattened, with a small spur at the base. They are typically green or bluish-green, measuring 10–15 mm, and remain on the plant even after dying, turning brown over time.<ref name="Eggli"/> The British population is distinguished by a compact and slow-growing rather than creeping [[habit (biology)|habit]], whereas the North African plants have distinctly bluish-purple foliage.<ref name="Stephenson"/> The species is [[evergreen]].<ref name="Missouri"/>
[[File:Sedum forsterianum flower (03).jpg|thumb|The flowers of ''P. forsterianum'' are arranged in clusters.]]
When in bloom, the flowering stems of ''Petrosedum forsterianum'' stand upright, reaching {{Convert|10-40|cm|4=0|abbr=on}}. The flowers are arranged in branching clusters ([[corymb]]s), with each branch curving downward while in bud before straightening as they open. The flowers usually have five to seven, sometimes up to nine, bright yellow [[petal]]s that spread outward. The [[sepal]]s, small leaf-like structures at the flower's base, are triangular with a pointed tip and grow up to 3 mm long. The [[stamen]]s, which produce [[pollen]], are also yellow.<ref name="Eggli"/> The peak of the flowering season is in early summer.<ref name="Smith"/> The plant produces upright [[seed capsule]]s that are pale brown with distinct ridges.<ref name="Eggli"/>

''Petrosedum forsterianum'' has a variable [[chromosome count]] (2n = 24, 48, 60, 72, or 96).<ref name="Eggli"/> A [[cristate]] form may be produced, but is much rarer than in ''P. rupestre''.<ref name="Stephenson"/>

==Use==
''Petrosedum forsterianum'' is edible. It can be added to salads and soups.<ref name="Kunkel">{{cite book | last=Kunkel | first=Günther | title=Plants for Human Consumption: An Annotated Checklist of the Edible Phanerogams and Ferns | publisher=Koeltz Scientific Books | year=1984 | isbn=978-3-87429-216-0 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7L0H0WBBMOkC&pg=PA333 | access-date=31 January 2025 | page=328}}</ref> It may also be used in [[green roof]]s.<ref name="Durham">{{cite journal | last1=Durhman | first1=Angela K. | last2=Rowe | first2=D. Bradley | last3=Rugh | first3=Clayton L. | title=Effect of Substrate Depth on Initial Growth, Coverage, and Survival of 25 Succulent Green Roof Plant Taxa | journal=HortScience | publisher=American Society for Horticultural Science | volume=42 | issue=3 | year=2007 | issn=0018-5345 | doi=10.21273/hortsci.42.3.588 | doi-access=free | pages=588–595 | url=https://journals.ashs.org/downloadpdf/journals/hortsci/42/3/article-p588.pdf | access-date=9 February 2025}}</ref> This plant adapts well to a range of soils as long as good drainage is provided, performing best in dry to moderately moist conditions with plenty of sunlight. It can handle partial shade and withstands both heat and humidity. It favors sandy or gravelly soil with minimal fertility. Over time, it will naturally expand in the garden.<ref name="Missouri">{{cite web | title=''Sedum forsterianum'' 'Oracle' | url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=269940&isprofile=0&gen=Sedum | access-date=10 February 2025}}</ref>

Apart from the British and [[diploid]] North African populations, this species spreads too aggressively for a typical [[rock garden]]. It works well as [[ground cover]], particularly when contained, such as in a pot. Although it self-seeds easily in other settings, it remains manageable. The British form is less aggressive, but it also produces fewer flowers and is less vibrant in color. During hot, dry summers with intense sunlight, ''P. forsterianum'' often withers and may break apart. If this happens, its tightly clustered rosettes can reestablish themselves once moisture returns. While fully hardy across temperate climates, it prefers shadier, wetter conditions than its close relatives.<ref name="Stephenson">{{cite book | last=Stephenson | first=Ray | title=Sedum: Cultivated Stonecrops | publisher=Timber Press | year=1994| isbn=978-1-60469-100-9 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P5GGPwAACAAJ | access-date=2 February 2025 | page=118-120}}</ref> Pests and diseases do not normally affect it, but slugs, snails, and [[scale insect]]s may attack.<ref name="Missouri"/>
